p:
Two vastly different approaches. The Clergy Council is activating clergy within that precinct and within the neighborhood and they activate their response to incidents and they’re proactive. The Wick in Bushwick is actually a scaled down version of a cure violence side if you will. That’s part of the approach that they do. In the cure violence in this work, of course we have the Cure Violence model that flows through that work as well. At times, we fund full catchments. In some cases, we fund half catchments. In the case of

the Wick, it is more of a hybrid of a half catchment. They’re doing an amazing job as you know out there. I think when it comes to the increase in funding, we need to look at the state of player things, the RFP’s, future RFP’s and future funded. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, so we don’t know. Okay but I’m glad - I’m encouraged to hear your take on it. It is really a valuable program and I mean the community has really felt like they’ve seen results like day to night. Bushwick houses had a record number of violent crimes. In 2015-2017, the MAP program came - the city selected Southside United and that work has really been wonderful and as the member representing that district to see young people involved in problem solving. To see young people involved in community activism, I think because of this crucial funding has been just beautiful and I would love to help. Would love to have you come Commissioner. I know you’re doing - listening towards insight visits but it’s really a wonderful thing led by really hard working people that are so committed, so, so committed and so of course, I’m always going to go to bat for them so they can get

more money to do this work. So, I would love to keep the conversation going. Thank you Chair.
Council Member Joseph. Welcome back.

Thank you. I was just on a commercial break. I’m back now. Welcome. Thank you for the work that God Squad does in my district. It’s so important, especially at the point where I lost a young person who was one of my students and it was God Squad that came and stood with me in the moment when I got the call from the mom. And what’s sad about it is the fact that it was a mistake in identity. He was 16. He was my fourth grade student. I raised them to go to graduation, not to a funeral. So, when they came and stood with me as a mom one, as a forever educator, it meant a lot. So, the work that they do in the 67th precinct is meaningful work and that’s why we support them so much. And Pastor Streker(SP?) was complaining about a tree I planted in front of the office. So, I told him, we’re going to pray together about that. So, uhm, I want to talk about headcount in the 2027 Preliminary Budget. DYCD supports 715 full time positions, an increase of 74 positions from Fiscal

2026 Adopted Budget. The Department Fiscal 2026 January actual headcount is 616. With the increased headcount of 74 since the adopted budget, what is the projected timeline for filling the positions?

Thank you for that question and uhm, we are pleased that we got to that headcount in the November plan and we started recruiting and hiring them. In fact, we filled about a dozen of those. The rest of them, a lot of them, most of them are posted on the website, the city’s website and we’re actively recruiting. Many of those, as I mentioned earlier, are to support the COMPASS expansion. So, our goal is to get them filled this spring so that they are ready, up and running for August.
Beautiful, thank you for that. Uhm, does the increased headcount of 74 represent permanent full time positions?
Yes, these are all full time.
Full time. What is the agency's current vacancy rate?
So, it’s a bit of - it’s overstated a little bit only because of this addition of the headcount. So, it’s currently at 15 percent with the new headcount.
What are the open positions for each of the programs that you have?

So, they are very - uh they expand the variety of the need for the agency. A lot of them in our fiscal shop to support some of the payments, the budget reviews for contracting and obviously a lot of direct program management.
Do you have a timeline to staff up to make sure those positions, those key positions are filled?
So, we’ve started filling a lot of the support functions because the contracting and the budget reviews are going to start up very soon and then program positions following.
Thank you. What agency asked to reduce the current vacancy in the preliminary plan.
Yes, we know that there is a central request from all agencies to reduce headcount.
So, what are the specific parameters of the headcount reduction if any?
We’re still working with OMB to figure out what the specific impact and details will be for our agency.
Will that impact the services that you provide?
We are advocating for it to be mitigated so that we don’t uh falter on delivering what we are supposed to be doing.

What challenges are the agencies facing in hiring new candidates? I know that's something that we hear from agencies a lot. Are you doing outreach? Where are you doing the outreach? Is it grassroot? Do other agencies - where?

The biggest challenge as you are probably aware was the two for one, which was recently lifted. So, we are seeing - you know we’ve always seen a lot of candidates apply for our positions. It was just kind of like the two for one that held us back from making those offers.
And how long does it take if someone applies for a position within your agency? How long does it take from applying to hiring?
It varies depending on the uhm I guess the complexity of the position and the number of people who are applying for those positions but I would say usually about a month.

About a month, 30 days. That’s good. In the Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Plan, the Administration had lifted the two to one that you mentioned earlier. What course of action is the agency taking to fill positions now that the rules are no longer applied?
I’m sorry, can you repeat that?

Sure, I said, uhm the two to one you talked about that model being lifted. For one of the every two vacant positions, what course of action is the agency taking to fill positions now that the rules no longer apply, your two to one?
So, we are working closely with OMB on that and I think that what helps is if we invite them invite candidates, that’s what speeds up the process.

And I had a quick follow up for Summer Rising. I know. I just wanted to know real quick. In working with students with disabilities, is there any interagency connections or any interagency work that you guys do? Because one of the biggest things I know Chair Stevens and I talk about is the fact that agencies don’t talk to each

other, which I think they should start talking to each other.

So, that is a great question. I’m actually excited to talk about the work we’ve been doing with New York City Public Schools over the past couple of years with their uh Office of Disability. I’m going to just say the acronym DIO. We’ve changed the names a couple of times. What’s been amazing is that like I said before, year to year there’s been massive improvements in not just the engagement with CBO’s but really thoughtful on trainings. So, there has been opportunities for asynchronous and in person trainings have been offered in collaboration with DYCD and New York City Public Schools. We’ve also implemented accommodation plans for a young person that gives an opportunity for a CBO and the teacher to have real time understanding of the actual young person's needs. You know, it is important to share that with an IEP, that’s information that can’t be shared to a CBO and that becomes a significant challenge and through this accommodation plan, it really speaks to how we can address the young persons needs and ensure that there

are services if needed for a young person into the afternoon hours.
I know at one point, you guys had a waiver on the IEP. Is that being shared at least with a PARA that can then relate to service to the child.

Yeah, so for those that are able legally to have access to the IEP, that is something that is provisioned to those selected folks but that accommodation plan is truly what is a document that can be of support for the CBO because really the CBO working in the afternoon is a key component because as we mentioned before, we want to make sure that all young people take full advantage of the program.
Okay wonderful, thank you so much.
No problem.

Okay, I’m back. Uhm, at an oversight hearing with the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education, the Deputy Chancellor spoke about a pilot program called School Day Plus, extending 3K to afterschool hours from 5-6. Have there been any conversations with DOE on what this could look like if there was after school for our

younger 3K students and has the agency began accessing the cost for providers?

I mean, I think that’s a great opportunity. It’s something that I’m going to be speaking with the Chancellor about because this idea of a continuous care service through early childhood through post-secondary is something that we’re eager to do under my leadership.

Advocates are concerned that two schools in the higher need school district 30 and PS 171 and PS 76 in Queens have an economic need indicator of 93 percent and due to the Leaps reconstructing did not receive additional seats for universal after school programs. Has this agency been aware of those school districts' concerns? Can the agency explain the process of determining who received the additional seats?

So, thank you for the question and as you know, since we’re in the middle of the act of procurement and a war process so there are limits what we can about specific schools at this stage. But what we can share is that this procurement was designed to target investments within specific geographic areas to strengthen continuity of

programming and expand services in communities with great needs.

What measures has the HD taken to address the mental health and social emotional learning as SCL programs in the RFP? What are the qualifications for SCL programs and what type of trainings will be provided? I know we spent a lot of time talking about this during our RFP process.

Yup, so you know supporting young people's mental health and social emotional development is a critical part of the model itself and we incorporated feedback from CBOs and stakeholders that strengthen these programmatic elements. So, this is inclusive of clarifying the mental health requirements, making social emotional learning a required content area within the program design itself. And the RFP also aligns the qualification and professional development expectations with the New York State SAC requirements, an inclusive training that supports youth with development and social emotional learning.
How is the agency measuring the success of the programs? How will they be measuring that?

So, success is measured by whether additional seats are directed to the highest need schools and whether you know the number of high need schools without free after school option decreases and whether enrollment and attendance patterns demonstrate that families are accessing the new seats. So, we also review provider readiness, program quality indicators, and feedback from school leaders and families.
How uhm, how many CBO provider services and training for their attendees and what is the budget for middle school Career Readiness program?
Could you repeat that first part?
Oh, the first question, I’m sorry. I’m starting to merge questions because we ran out of time. Sorry about that.
Yeah, I know.
How many CBOs providers have training uhm, been training - trainings for their attendees? How many service providers have been giving trainings for their attendees?

So, since we are in the procurement stage, it’s a little bit challenging to identify like the you and the existing providers that would be providing these trainings but it is the expectation that all providers will be doing support from these areas.

Hmm, hmm. The new COMPASS RFP, the rates for SONIC middle school program were set at $3,900 uhm only a $700 difference from the $3,200 rates set ten years ago. Does DYCD have a model budget that can show the matrix using to making this decision on how providers will make sure that those rates work with the mandated program requirements?
I think we expand on that. I think that when it comes to the model budget, that’s dependent upon the CBO but we can have conversations about how that is done, about how the costs are determined.

Yeah, I mean, I have some legislation that I’ve been trying to push around like, I feel like when we put out these RFP’s, we should be doing a model budget so programs could see what our thinking is behind it because sometimes these numbers just don’t match and it’s like, how are we supposed to do this and so, I think some providers would appreciate if we could like get an idea of what you’re thinking around like salaries and things like that of like how they’re supposed to make it work.
We can take that into consideration for future procurements.

Yeah and not just this - and I’ve been doing this - I’ve been talking about this for all of them and you know I’ve been getting a lot of push back on it but I’m going to start pushing that legislation again. Uhm, has there been any additional discussion about bringing back COMPASS Explorers program?
Well, we have limited resources right now Chair Stevens and so.
Not for the babies.

I think we have experienced in fatherhood in literacy and COMPASS and so, the city

is continuing to invest. I’m not sure if we will have the funding to restore the COMPASS Explorer program.

Well, I will say this. If we invest in our kids on the front end, we don’t have to invest in them on the back end and Explorers is one of those programs that we invest, making an investment so we don’t have to put young people in detention and again, because those numbers are rising and it’s very costly when kids are in detention. I think that actually if we’re thinking about savings, we should be providing all the programs, so that they’re not ending up in detention. So, I will continue to be on my one woman crusade to make sure we have programming for these young people. I’m going to move into Advance and Earn. Uhm, is that Val? Is she coming? Is she coming over here? Don’t worry Susan, you’re coming up, so HRY is coming up, don’t worry. I don’t know why you all keep using these seats. There’s three seats over here. They don’t like you, Nevita. I don’t know what’s going on with you over there but you must be the mean one or something.

What is the total budget in Fiscal 2027 for the Advance Earn learning program?

Sure, so I’ll take that for you Valerie. Uhm, Advance and Earn program, just give me one second, I can give you the budget. Advance and Earn budget in FY26 is $22 million, in FY27 $22 million annually.
What are the number of providers in the Advance and Earn program?
Thank you for that question.
Hello.
Nice to see you.
Did we swear you in?
Hmm?
Did we swear you in?
Yes.
Okay, great.

And thank you for getting to workforce development. So, the Advance and Earn program has five community based organizations who collectively run seven distinct programs. There’s three programs in the Bronx and then one program in each other borough.
Has the agency seen an increase or decrease in the number of young adults attending the Advance and Earn program and what do those numbers look like?

Yes, we have. I know in the past we’ve discussed about how challenging it is to recruit the OSOW population. We have seen that number increase. This year we’re fully enrolled in the Advance and Earn program. We have over 1,300 young people who are - our first cohort was in September. That cohort completed. It was fully enrolled and then we just started our second cohort, also fully enrolled and we are excited. We were able to receive additional resources from ACS, so, we’ve expanded the Doors program to be able to serve referrals who come from ACS. And so, we’ve been able to increase that number even more.
Okay. uhm, which boroughs and districts have the highest attendance rates for the Advance and Earn?

Alright, so I have it right here because my team was texting it to me in live time. The Bronx is 34 percent of our participants,

Brooklyn 23 percent, Queens 20 percent, Manhattan 14 percent and Staten Island 9 percent.
Okay. Alright, we’re going to go onto Work, Learn and Grow. What is the current enrollment in Work, Learn and Grow program?

Great so Work, Learn, and Grow currently has 6,500 young people enrolled with 55 SYEP providers and then an additional 1,190 young people enrolled through our Learn and Earn providers. So, we are well over our target goal of 7,000 young people a year.
What is the current budget for the program and is it significant? What is the current budget for the program and what is the differences?
Baseline budget for Work, Learn and Grow was $30 million.
Okay, what is the recruitment process for Work, Learn and Grow programs and how many youth applied for the program in Fiscal 2026?

Sure, so Work, Learn, and Grow is a direct recruitment program, meaning that our providers both in the SYEP and Learn and Earn

portfolio are identifying young people who participated in Summer Youth Employment Program. So, we do this in a couple of ways. We do it through our Career Ready SYEP model where the providers work directly with schools that they’re partnered with to identify young people. We do it through our Special Initiatives Career Ready Program, which as you know is our emerging leaders in our NYCHA contracts where our providers are working with their partners in those spaces to identify young people and then every young person who enrolled in Learn and Earn, which is OEO funded in School Youth Program has an opportunity to participate.

Hold on a second. In 2025, the annual report of 100,000 SYEP reserved for Summer 2026, that included partnership with the city agencies and CBOs. How many city agencies participated in the program and how many CBOs participated in the program?
Sorry, the question was how many city agencies and how many?
CBOs.

CBOs, so we fund 65 community based organizations in the SYEP program but our goal

is to have placements in every single city agency. I can get you the report of how many young people are placed at each agency.

Yes, that would be very helpful because that was some of the - I actually did a bill to support to make sure that uhm, that age city agencies were actually participating in SYEP because we found when I came that a lot agencies were not participating to my surprise. Uhm, so the next question. Does the agency have a plan to target for SYEP and what does the number look like?
I don’t know why I’m having so much of a hard time hearing. Can you hear?
Listen, no, I don’t have both mics. Is that better?
I’ll do my best.
Uhm, I said, does the agency have plans to grow the target SYEP program and what does the number look like if they do?
So, you’re talking - does the agency have a plan to expand SYEP?
Yeah.

Yes, okay. So, we’re about to approach our 5th summer, reaching 100,000 young people. That is our goal for the summer. We’re really proud of it. Uhm, as you know the largest youth employment program in the country and I think it’s something New York City should be really proud of. Uhm, we do have a really high number of applications. You know last year's application number closed at 209,000 and so, we know that there are young people who apply to the program and don’t get in and in a world of limited resources, we think really hard about how we maximize the resources we do have to reach as many of the young people as possible. So, not only targeting in the ways of like in NYCHA, in our Emerging Leaders program, but also thinking about how young people who aren’t fully engaged in the program, if they don’t show up are we able to use those resources to bring another young person off of the waitlist so that we can really make sure we’re reaching as many as possible.

Uhm, and with all that being said, uhm, my concern is right now, when we’re looking at youth unemployment rates, we’re at 13.2

percent and Black Youth specifically are at 23.8 percent and those numbers are really astonishing and also, we have to understand why Black youth are not being employed throughout the city. And so, thinking about how are we using those numbers to really target these populations and to ensure that they have employment. I mean, my suggestion is one, we need full year programming around employment. That’s my goal but how are we even using the programs that we have like Earn and Learn and SYEP and Work, Learn and Grow to kind of address these numbers that are showing that young people are having a hard time finding employment. And even how are we looking at this 23 percent of Black youth not having employment?

Yeah, that’s a great question and it’s something we think about all the time. You know that through all of our workforce programs, we have been moving to be as intentional about recruitment as possible. I do want to share that in SYEP, 37 percent of our participants are Black and 30 percent are Hispanic, so I think we do do a really good job of doing outreach and these are numbers we’ve seen grow year over year as we’re increasing

our investments in the special priority populations and we would have some learn numbers in any one of our workforce programs and I think there’s more we can keep doing there. So, I agree with you.

Yeah, I think we have to definitely be targeted in making sure that we’re constantly looking at those numbers to monitor it and think about it. Has the agency started conversations with CBOs and city agencies and other potential partners in starting our year around employment program for youth? If so, what would that program look like if you’ve had those conversations? Listen, I’m always about dreaming big and if we’re not planning for it, then it ain’t going to happen.

I think we share the same dream and I think we have it. I think Work, Learn and Grow is a really impactful and successful model and I think uh what we want to look at is how we can leverage the things that we’ve learned from Work, Learn and Grow. Like, the way that we’ve been able to leverage resources from public schools and CUNY to expand the offerings within that program in an efficient way, which has allowed us to continue to

scale and add quality at the same time and I think that’s the place to look because i think that pipeline of SYEP to Work, Learn and Grow has been really effective and is something we can continue to build off of.

Why is there a disconnect in the number of applications and the number of youth with jobs? So, there’s such a disconnect in how high the numbers are for the applications or having in the jobs that they have. Can you talk a little bit about that and like, what are doing to kind of look at that?

Yeah, uhm, it’s a great question. I think - I think a couple of things. I think uhm for me personally, it means that the program has been really successful because we’ve seen the number of applications grow exponentially year over year and of course there is an element of need that is behind that but there is also an element of word of mouth and I see this as young people telling their friends that if you need a job or a place to go over the summer, that SYEP is that place. So, I’m really proud of that number because I think we’ve done a really good job making SYEP a

popular program for young people and it’s where they come. At the same time, I think we all sit with that really big application number and wonder how are we ever going to reach the need. I don’t think the need is the full application number. Every year, we have to make multiple offers in order to fill each slot, right? But I do know that there are young people who aren’t going to get into the program and so we are constantly - it’s something I’ve already started talking to our Commissioner about how we’re going to think about meeting that need.
DYCD testified that they uhm, that they have two SYEP evaluations at the middle of the program and one at the end. What information does the survey provide? Like, what did it provide for you guys?

Yes, so we implement two surveys throughout the SYEP program. One towards the beginning of the program and one at the end of the program. The one at the beginning of the program, assesses a young person's experience enrolling in the program, their orientation experience, their experience with Hats and Ladders, which is our like preemployment curriculum. That’s where our financial

literacy curriculum is and then at the end of the program, we’re assessing, were you satisfied with the program? Did you have a good summer? Did you meet a mentor? Did you meet an adult that you learned something from? It’s a really substantial, lots of questions. We do it in partnership with our evaluation team here. And, I will say, my team takes those surveys really seriously because of their direct feedback from young people.

Is this survey provided to all folks who attend SYEP or is it like limited to like a select number? And has the agency - and how does the agency take uhm that feedback and use that to continue to roll out and shape the programs?

Yeah, uh so the survey is offered - any young person who participates in the program is able to take this survey. We do a big email blast. We remind them. We ask our providers to reach out to their young people. So, we really try to get as many responses to the survey as possible, and we do take their feedback really seriously. I can give you one direct example. Uhm, we had heard year over year that one of the concerns with the younger youth model is that it was very

virtual and we started to see in the data and in responses from young people that they wanted more in person, out of their house activity. And so, this year, we have moved to require that 50 percent of those programs will be in person as a direct response to what we were seeing in that survey data.
And especially with the middle school, did they also talk about the 700,000 stipend that they don’t like? Was that some of their feedback as well?

Uhm, look, I think we believe in that model as a concept right? We do think that it’s really uhm, it is as a program policy, it makes a lot of sense that a young person's first experience isn’t good. Like a 14 year old shouldn’t have the same experience as a 24 year old. And so, we believe in the model. We, you know believe it or not, have really high satisfaction rates with that model. I think 95 percent of the participants who responded, who are younger youth participants, said that we were satisfied or very satisfied.
With the $700?
With the program overall.
Oh, no I was talking about the $700. That’s the thing that I’m trying ot -
I hear you.
Come on.

The $700 is a part of their overall experience right? And so if you just take a step back and think about how a young person is telling us, DYCD, whether they enjoyed the program or not, we’re getting really positive feedback and we have way more than enough applications to fill those slots, so it’s not like we have a lack of young people filling those slots. With that said, we are always looking at the models really closely and talking to our partners at OMB about where we see areas for improvement.

Yeah, let’s start with the $700. Let’s see an area of improvement there because I think we can laugh about it but we know that a young person who’s 14, 15, how vulnerable they are and when we uhm offer them $700 and then other folks can offer them $1,000, they’re going to take that and I think that that is important and that brings me to the next question.

Last year, we had a huge scandal around debit cards and those young people were vulnerable and they sold it because guess what, if I offered you a $1,000 for your card and you only gave me $700, I’m like, here you go. So, that is a place where we can see in real time that it is not enough. And so, they can say they’re satisfied with the program but clearly it’s not enough. And so, what are we doing to make sure that - to ensure that that doesn’t happen this year and like what are next steps? Just to also secure the safety of young people.

Yeah, look, obviously we were extremely concerned and if I can even say devastated about what happened last summer and we moved immediately. Our priority was first and foremost to protect the participants and then also to protect the integrity of the program, which we hold really dear. And so, after we got through the initial kind of crisis of last summer, we started looking really closely at all of our policies and procedures. That summer, we made many referrals to DOI and NYPD and we have been following all of their guidance but we also worked with our payroll vendor to assess all of the

controls in place to better understand what they are doing to work with the banks to make sure that they’ve put all of the controls that are necessary in place and you know from my team, our responsibility at DYCD is also to ensure that we’re monitoring our providers and putting policies in place that they are able to follow and that we’re issuing corrective action plans where we see any vulnerabilities caused by our providers. And so, we’ve been working with our team at DYCD to implement that. Every safe measure that we can to protect the program this year.

Thank you. Uhm, I do know that last summer, you guys acted very swiftly and was trying to mitigate the entirety. So, but you know I always want us to be thinking about how do we prevent things moving forward because we just don’t want that to happen again. And that is it for you, so thank you so much. We’re going to be talking about HRY, so I’m assuming Susan will be coming up. Oh, it’s not you anymore. Oh, look at that. Look at this.
They’re throwing me out there.

Okay, for Fiscal 2027 Preliminary Plan did not include additional funding

for RHY programming. Has DYCD had conversations with OMB to fund and rightsize those programs?

Chair Stevens, we’re always in conversations with OMB about rightsizing programs. Uhm, as you know, we’re in a Fiscal crisis and we’re trying to figure out how we can identify savings. So, we’ll continue to have conversations but we’re not there yet.

The Administration provided baseline funding for $6 million in FY26 Preliminary Budget for 100 beds for homeless young adults, ages 21 and 24 at the rate of 49,000 to 50,000 per bed. The additional beds were a win, so thank you. However, providers are advocating for the rate of 70K per bed to ensure that providers - to provide - for providers to offer the needed level of services for RHY requirements. Has the agency had a conversation with providers for additional funding to support the ask for 70K per bed?

We’re still working with OMB. I think that when it comes to procurement, we have to wait for the new RFP and that’s why we used the rates that we did for those existing 100 beds because they

are in the existing contracts that those providers had. As we transition into the new procurement for HRY and we determine the cost, we will try to see how we can increase that rate.

Yeah, I think that is really important and listen, no one was loud about those beds then me and so, you know, I don’t want to take away from the win because I remember our last OMB Director was like, Althea, every time I give you something, you come back with a new ask. But, I do but you know I think we have to make sure that we’re working with providers so that they can provide quality service as well. What is the current RHY budget and when was the last budget increase with the expansion of this $6 million per Fiscal Year?

Well, all contracts receive additional funding for ICI and COLA. So, the city has been making small incremental changes to providers' baselined funding for a number of years. Regarding the RHY portfolio, we have not done any substantial increases to it because we haven’t done

any new procurements but currently the baseline budget for the portfolio is about $63 million.
Can the agency update us on the status of 100 beds distributed. Where were they distributed geographically and how many if any have all been occupied?
I’m going to defer to Associate Commissioner Wanda Ascherl.

Good afternoon. Look at the time. Uhm, okay, so yes, we allocated 100 beds across 7 sites. We actually issued a survey to gather provider interests and we had about one, two, three, four, five, six - five providers that responded but again, we were able to allocate 100 beds at 7 sites. 50 of them have already - are operational. 50 of the beds are already operational at 4 locations and then, the other 50 are in varying stages of coming online including OCFS certifications. Uhm, having the space uhm checked to make sure that it’s safe and then just working with the various landlords to make sure that it’s something that’s reasonable for the provider. And then you asked me about where. Uhm, most of the new beds were allocated to Manhattan, Staten

Island, and Brooklyn. Uhm, based on the provider feedback but overall, there are a total of 264 beds in the Bronx and 293 beds in Manhattan. Those are the two -
But that’s not for older youth right? You’re just talking about the beds in general?
Yes, hmm, hmm.
Could you break it down by older youth and younger youth?
Yup, I can. Hmm, hmm. I can share that. I think uhm, I can share it by crises or maybe can I share it afterwards?

Yeah. So, I know advocates are advocating for $22.1 million from the state funding for RHY. Uhm if the state does not provide additional funding will the agency evaluate ways of providing additional supports for RHY? Especially for like housing navigators, case managing, uhm, and if we don’t get this from the state, like what are we going to do?

So, the city has been providing additional resources for the RHY portfolio annually with the housing navigator, so the financial uhm,
